On the one hand, it holds out to man the promise of great success, but on the other hand, its acceptance places man temporarily at risk: there is the fear of losing one’s worldly position; of clashing with the conventional set-up. God’s word as revealed to His prophets affects them similarly. They swore that they were of the believers while they were not, and there the chapter leaves them.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Or like a rainstorm in the sky, bringing darkness, thunder, and lightning. The choice of two examples is meant to divide the hypocrites into two kinds of men. They thrust their fingers in their ears to keep out the stunning thunderclap for fear of death. And if Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and their sight. In the course of these parables, the hypocrites have also been warned that they are not beyond the power of Allah, and that He can, as and when He likes, take away their sight and hearing, and even destroy them. Certainly, Allah has power over all things This is another parable which Allah gave about the hypocrites who sometimes know the truth and doubt it at other times. When they suffer from doubt, confusion and disbelief, their hearts are, (Like a Sayyib), meaning, "The rain", as Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, and several other Companions have confirmed as well as Abu Al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr, 'Ata', Al-Hasan Al-Basri, Qatadah, 'Atiyah Al-'Awfi, 'Ata' Al-Khurasani, As-Suddi and Ar-Rabi' bin Anas. " However, the most accepted opinion is that it means the rain that comes down during,

21.text:
The sūrah has finished telling the reader who receives this book and who refuses it, and now the address widens to everyone: "O humanity, Worship your Lord", and the reason attached to the command is not a threat but a fact about them, "Who created you and those before you", and then the purpose, "so that you may become mindful of Him". The sources take the call as general in wording and particular in who first heard it, and that the same address carries both, since a claim about creation is not limited to the generation standing in front of the Prophet. Then the order of the sentence is taken up: worship is asked for before anything is promised, and the one who is asked is told only what He is to them, that He made them and made those before them, which is the plainest possible reason and the only one the verse uses. The word for worship is read as a harmony with the command rather than a performance, and the mindfulness at the end is the effect the whole verse aims at, not a reward added to it. That is why these words are placed here: the chapter has spent twenty verses dividing people by how they answer a claim about God, and now the claim itself is set in front of them all, with the evidence of it in the sky and the earth, which is the verse that follows. One line of the sources presses the phrase "those before you", since the verse names only the generations that came earlier, leaving what comes after them unaddressed here, and that is deliberate, because a people who had watched earlier generations perish could not turn away from that argument.

**An address to all humanity.**

He means to say that the expression (O mankind!) is an address to the people of Makkah while (O ye who believe!) is an address to the people of Medina. Hence, Allah's saying (O mankind! Worship your Lord) is an address to the Meccan idolaters. (O mankind!) O people of Makkah; and it is also said that this refers to the Jews, (Worship your Lord), declare Him as the only One God, (Who hath created you) as different lineages beginning from a drop of sperm, (and those before you) just as He created those who came before you, (so that ye may ward off) so that you may ward off His wrath and torment and obey Him. O people of Makkah worship profess the oneness of your Lord Who created you made you when you were nothing and created those that were before you; so that you may be fearful of His punishment by worshipping Him la‘alla ‘so that’ is essentially an optative but when spoken by God it denotes an affirmative.

**What worship is.**

Worship ʿibāda is becoming harmonious muwāfaqa with the command and it is pouring all energy into requests for realization taḥqīq of the unseen. It is said worship Him by renouncing prohibited things persevering in performing acts of obedience welcoming obligatory acts with humility and lowliness and avoiding detours through the waystations of laziness and indifference. And the message delivered by the verse is:' "Worship your Lord.

**Created you, and those before you.**

In adding to the phrase: :"who created you" the words, ; and those before you," the verse shows that Allah alone is the Creator of all mankind. It is also significant that the verse mentions only "those before you" and not "those who will come after you", and through this omission suggests that there will not be any Ummah (a traditional community formed by all the followers of a prophet) to succeed the Ummah of the Holy Prophet for no prophet will be sent down after the Last Prophet and hence no new Ummah' will arise. Worship your Lord (Allah), Who created you and those who were before you so that you may acquire Taqwa Who has made the earth a resting place for you, and the sky as a canopy, and sent down water (rain) from the sky and brought forth therewith fruits as a provision for you. O people, worship no one other than your Lord, because He created you and the people before you, so that you may save yourselves from suffering, by following His instructions and keeping away from what He has prohibited.

**So that you may become mindful of Him.**

His saying so that you may be fearful is to bring the command closer to them and to make it easier. But since He is invisible, it often happens that man gives importance to some visible object and worships that instead of God. They have become so greatly attached to their supposed ‘deities’ that they cannot believe that they are unreal. The verse was revealed about the believers as well as those it reproaches, which is how the chapter keeps its first hearers inside every command.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The second verse of the Surah 'Al-Baqarah' provides the answer to the prayer made in the Surah Al-Fatihah, ‌ "Guide us in the straight path"- that is to say, the guidance man has prayed for is present in this book, for the Holy Qur'an is from the beginning to the end a detailed account of the straight path. Then, the Surah proceeds to divide men into three groups according to whether they accept the guidance of the Holy Qur'an or not. Three verses speak of the true and God-fearing Muslims, who not only accept but also act upon the guidance, and the next two verses of those disbelievers who oppose it openly. Then come thirteen verses dealing with the hypocrites who are hostile to this guidance, but, for the sake of petty worldly interests or in seeking to harm the Muslims, try to keep their disbelief concealed and to present themselves as Muslims. Thus, the first twenty verses of the Surah, in dividing men into three groups on the basis of their acceptance or rejection of the guidance, indicate that the proper criterion for dividing men into groups is neither race or colour, nor language nor geography, but religion.

22.text:
The evidence for the claim about worship arrives at once, and it is all around the person being asked: "He is the One Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy", then "and sends down rain from the sky", then "causing fruits to grow as a provision for you". The verse moves from what is under the feet to what is over the head and then to what comes between the two, and the sources take that order as the point of the sentence, because each of the three is a thing a person uses without ever being able to make it. The word used for the earth is read as a thing spread out for rest, a bed rather than solid ground, and the sky as a roof that is held up, and the rain is what makes the two useful at the same time, since it is the water that turns hard soil into food. Then the verse draws its conclusion itself, "So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah in worship", and the emphasis on knowingly is the whole weight of it, since a person who has been shown all of this and still shares the worship has not been misled by evidence they lacked but by a thing they recognised and set aside. This is why the verse stands where it does: the worship asked for in the verse above rests on a proof that does not require scripture, and the challenge in the verse after it will go the other way, from what cannot be produced to what cannot be doubted.

**The earth as a place of settlement.**

He Who assigned to you created for you the earth for a couch like a carpet that is laid out neither extremely hard nor extremely soft so as to make it impossible to stand firm upon it; and heaven for an edifice like a roof; and sent down from the heaven water wherewith He brought forth all types of fruits for your provision; so set not up compeers to God that is partners in worship while you know that He is the Creator that you create not and that only One that creates can be God. He made the earth a resting place for them, just like the bed, stable with the firm mountains. (Who hath appointed the earth a resting-place for you), a place for dwelling and sleeping, (and the sky a canopy), raised high above; (and causeth water to pour down from the sky), i.e. rain, (thereby producing) through this rain (fruits) different kinds of fruit (as food for you) as sustenance for you and all created beings. It is He Who made the earth like a carpet spread out in front of you and it is He Who masterfully constructed the sky over you.

**The sky as a canopy.**

About the one He says, ["We set in heaven constellations] and We adorned them for the gazers" [15:16] and about the other He says, ["And earth,] We laid it out-what excellent spreaders!" [51:48]. Hence, whoever gazes at the sky in its immensity, its expanse, and the various kinds of planets in it, some of which appear stationary in the sky - whoever gazes at the seas that surround the land from all sides, and the mountains that were placed on the earth to stabilize it, so that whoever lives on land, whatever their shape and color, are able to live and thrive - whoever reads Allah's statement,. He has invested the world with profound significance and He constantly looks after its needs.

**Rain, and fruits as provision.**

But the Holy Qur'an has, in certain verses, made it quite clear that human effort has nothing to do with the act of growing trees and bringing out fruits, for human activity accomplishes nothing more than removing the hindrances to the birth and growth of a plant, or protecting it from being destroyed. Hence, Allah caused the various types of vegetation and fruits to grow as a means of sustenance for people and their cattle. Through His grace rain falls, producing different crops from the earth, as produce for you.

**Do not knowingly set up equals.**

(So do not set up rivals to Allah) do not say that Allah has peers, different forms or coequals (when you know) that He is the fashioner of all these things. It is also said that (when you know) means: when you know from your own scripture that Allah does not have a son, coequal or peer. Do not, then, consider others to be equal to Allah, when you know that He alone is worthy of being worshipped. But since He is invisible, it often happens that man gives importance to some visible object and worships that instead of God.

**What the two verses call people to.**

To sum up, these two verses call men to what is the essential purpose of sending down all the Divine Books and all the prophets – Tauhid or the affirmation and the worship of the one God. Having learnt from these two verses that it is Allah, and no one else, who brings man into existence out of nothingness, and provides the means of his sustenance through the earth, the sky, the rains and the fruits, one cannot, if one possesses a little common sense, help acknowledging that Allah, and no one else, is worthy of all worship and obedience, and that the ultimate iniquity is to turn away from Him who made man exist and gave him the means of survival and growth, and to prostrate oneself before others who are as helpless as man. He who made for you the earth a carpet and the heaven a building, and who sent down from heaven water by which He brought forth fruits for you as provision. How pure and faultless is the God who brought forth the brightness of day from the pitch black night and made the darkness of the pitch black night appear from the brightness of day! Worship your Lord (Allah), Who created you and those who were before you so that you may acquire Taqwa Who has made the earth a resting place for you, and the sky as a canopy, and sent down water (rain) from the sky and brought forth therewith fruits as a provision for you. A partner is denied on grounds the hearer can inspect, and the next verse turns to a refusal that will not be persuaded.

**What else the same passage holds.**

That is to say, once one has understood that, in reality, Allah alone is the Creator and the Provider, one will have also understood that no one else can be worthy of worship and of being associated with Allah as an equal or rival god. Tauhid is a doctrine which has an all-pervading and radically transforming impact on every sphere of human life, internal as well as external, individual as well as collective. For, once a man comes to believe that there is only One Being who alone is the Creator, the Lord and Master of the universe, who alone is all-powerful and ordains the slightest movement of the smallest atom, and without whose will no one can harm or do good to another - such a man, rich or poor, in joy or sorrow, would always look only towards that One Being, and gain the insight to discover behind the veil of apparent causes the workings of the same Omnipotence.

23.text:
The chapter now puts the case where it can be tested, "And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant", and the demand that follows is deliberately small, "then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah", on one condition only, "if what you say is true". The sources stop on the size of the challenge, since a book was being answered with a single sūrah, and the answer they give is that the point is not the length of the task but the thing the task would prove: if the words are like these words, then a person has made them. The description of the Prophet as "Our servant" is taken up as its own argument, because the claim being tested is that this speech came through a servant, and the challenge leaves no third position between that and a forgery. Then the phrase "call your helpers" is read as the generosity in the verse rather than its difficulty, since they were invited to bring whoever they wanted, from their jinn and their people, and the sources list the enemies who tried and did not, which is the part of this passage the chapter keeps coming back to. The verse stands between a proof in the sky and the earth, which anyone can see, and a proof in speech, which the people who prided themselves on speech could not produce, and the next verse closes the door on trying again.

**The challenge, and how small it was made.**

And if you are in doubt in uncertainty concerning what We have revealed to Our servant Muhammad of the Qur’ān that it is from God then bring a sūra like it that is also revealed min mithlihi min is explicative that is a sūra like it in its eloquence fine arrangement and its bestowal of knowledge of the Unseen; a sūra is a passage with a beginning and end made up of a minimum of three verses; and call your witnesses those other gods that you worship besides God that is other than Him so that it can be seen if you are truthful in your claim that Muhammad speaks it from himself. Allah challenges those who have any doubt about the Qur’ān revealed to His servant, Muhammad ﷺ, to produce a chapter just like it, and to call their helpers, if they are truthful about what they say. Hence, if you claim that what he was sent with did not come from Allah, then produce something similar to what he has brought to you, using the help of anyone you wish instead of Allah. So do this for you are also fluent speakers of Arabic like him.

**Why it was put to a people of speech.**

(And if ye are in doubt concerning that which We revealed) through the Archangel Gabriel (unto Our slave) Muhammad whom you accuse of fabrication, (then produce a surah like it) produce a surah like the surah of the Cow (al-Baqarah), (and call your witnesses), seek help from the gods that you worship, (apart from Allah), it is said that this refers to their leaders, (if ye are truthful) in your claim. This helplessness in a contest which should have been easy for a people so gifted with a spontaneous eloquence - does it not argue that the Holy Qur'an is not the word of man, but the Word of Allah? As for the people who hesitate in accepting the Holy Qur'an as the Word of Allah, and suspect that it is the work of the Holy Prophet or of some other man, the verse proposes an easy test - they should produce a passage (a Surah) resembling or equalling the Holy Qur'an in order to substantiate their claim; but if they fail, they should finally acknowledge the Holy Qur'an to be undoubtedly the Word of Allah.

**Call your helpers other than Allah.**

" Also, As-Suddi reported that Abu Malik said the Ayah means, "Your partners, meaning, some other people to help you in that. Even the vilest enemies of the Holy Prophet like Akhnas ibn Shariq, Abu Sufyan and, of all persons, Abu Jahl himself are reported to have stealthily crept in the darkness of night to the house of the Holy Prophet to hear him reciting the Holy Qur'an, and to have been so entranced by the Word of Allah that they could not tear themselves away from the place till it was dawn. This verse is an affirmation of prophecy, an argument against the Folk of the Book and the Dhimma.

**The servant named in the verse.**

As long as the servant does not acknowledge and believe in both and does not act as demanded by both, he has not entered into the circle of the submission. You take his words, deeds, customs, and conduct as your leader and guide. They cannot believe that the truth is what is proclaimed by a mortal just like themselves.

**Those who hesitated, and those who could not answer.**

The number of people hostile to Islam has, in any age, been much larger than that of Muslims, and they have possessed far greater and much more efficacious means of publicity than Muslims ever have. How can anyone be able to produce something like the Qur'an, when the Qur'an is the Word of Allah Who created everything? The prophets taught man to glorify God alone, and forsake the other things that he had elevated to a position of glory. People whose hearts are attached to objects other than God consider the call of true religion repugnant. The doubt here is about a book in front of them, which is why the next verse is a verdict.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The Guidance which the Holy Qur'an provides to man rests on two basic principles - Tauhid (the Oneness of God) and Risalah (Prophethood). The two preceding verses (21 and 22) affirm the Oneness of God in presenting certain acts peculiar to Allah alone as a proof; these two verses (23 and 24) affirm the prophethood of Muhammad in presenting the word of Allah as a proof.

24.text:
The verdict follows without a pause: "But if you are unable to do so", and then a clause that closes the future as well as the past, "and you will never be able to do so", and then what is asked of them instead, "then fear the Fire fuelled with people and stones". The sources take the middle clause first, because it is the one that looks unfair, and the reading given is that this is a statement of what they will not do rather than a prevention of their doing it, since the verse has already put the attempt in their hands. Then the fuel is the difficulty, and the word is read as whatever feeds a fire, so that stones are named alongside people rather than instead of them, and the commentators ask which stones and get no single answer, while one line takes the harder meaning, that a fire which consumes what cannot burn has no need of anything to keep it alight. Then the last phrase, "which is prepared for the disbelievers", is the link back to the verse before this one, since the doubt in that verse has now become the thing the verse is about. The spiritual reading puts the whole passage to another use and asks what a person should take from a fire whose fuel is stones, and the answer is that the warning is not there to be argued with, and signs and warners do not move a people who have decided not to be moved.

**The attempt and the refusal to repeat it.**

And if you do not do what was mentioned because you are incapable and you will not a parenthetical statement that is never will you be able to because of its inimitability then fear through belief in God and belief that this is not the words of a human the Fire whose fuel is men disbelievers and stones like their very idols indicating that its heat is extreme since it burns with the stones mentioned unlike the fires of this world that burn with wood and similar materials; prepared and made ready for disbelievers so that they are punished in it this phrase u‘iddat li’l-kāfirīna ‘prepared for disbelievers’ is either a new sentence or a sustained circumstantial qualifier. (But if you do it not, and you can never do it), indicating that they will never be able to answer the challenge. He said If you do not and then stated that they could not and would not do it for He said and you will not.

**A fire whose fuel is people and stones.**

It appears most obvious that it refers to the Fire that is fueled by men and stones, and it also may refer to the stones themselves. If they are unable to do so – and they will never be able to do it – they should be mindful of the fire of Hell, which burns with people who deserve the torment, and with the idols which they used to worship instead of Allah: punishing both the idol-worshipers and what they worshiped. If stones with all their hardness cannot withstand this fire how can men with their weakness bear itḍ When the hearts of the believers became terribly concerned from hearing mention of the fire He strengthened them and said prepared for disbelievers.

**What the stones are.**

(And if ye do it not-and you can never do it-) this you can never do and if you try you will never succeed (then guard yourselves against the Fire) if you are bent on not believing, for you should fear hell (whose fuel is men) the unbelievers, (and stones) of sulphur, (prepared) created, prepared and preordained (for disbelievers). The fire of Hell has been prepared as a punishment for the disbelievers. As for the people who hesitate in accepting the Holy Qur'an as the Word of Allah, and suspect that it is the work of the Holy Prophet or of some other man, the verse proposes an easy test - they should produce a passage (a Surah) resembling or equalling the Holy Qur'an in order to substantiate their claim; but if they fail, they should finally acknowledge the Holy Qur'an to be undoubtedly the Word of Allah.

**Doubt, and the word used for it.**

According to Imam Raghib al-Isfahani, raib ‌ signifies a kind of hesitation or indecision or suspicion which has no basis, and can therefore be easily overcome with the help of a little reflection. This helplessness in a contest which should have been easy for a people so gifted with a spontaneous eloquence - does it not argue that the Holy Qur'an is not the word of man, but the Word of Allah? Hence, if you claim that what he was sent with did not come from Allah, then produce something similar to what he has brought to you, using the help of anyone you wish instead of Allah. And if you (Arab pagans, Jews, and Christians) are in doubt concerning that which We have sent down (i.e. the Qur'an) to Our servant (Muhammad), then produce a Surah (chapter) of the like thereof and call your witnesses (supporters and helpers) besides Allah, if you are truthful But if you do it not, and you can never do it, then fear the Fire (Hell) whose fuel is men and stones, prepared for the disbelievers.

**A warning, not a caprice.**

The proper course for a man is to take God as his Creator, Master and Sustainer, and not attempt to set up anyone as a partner with Him; that is, a man should give himself up entirely to God. God most high said But signs and warners do not avail a folk who will not believe [10:101]. The next verse fore-warns them that such a venture would never succeed, and threatens with the fires of hell, for having once acknowledged his inability to produce something to equal the Holy Qur'an, which is a clear evidence of its being the word, not of man but of a Being who stands above all created things, if a man still persists in his disbelief, he is only seeking a place in hell. An inability known beforehand, described since the challenge; the next verse turns from the fire.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The Guidance which the Holy Qur'an provides to man rests on two basic principles - Tauhid (the Oneness of God) and Risalah (Prophethood).

25.text:
The chapter turns, and it turns quickly: the last two verses were about a fire and the only way to escape it, and this one opens with good news, "Give good news O Prophet to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow". The two halves of the previous description of the disbelievers are answered one by one, and this verse does the same, since belief and good works are set together, and what they are given is a garden with water under it rather than a fire above it. Then the verse stops on an odd detail, "Whenever provided with fruit", "they will say", "This is what we were given before", and the sources argue about what "before" means, whether it is what they were provided with in this world and so recognisable, or what they were promised in the sūrah and so fulfilled, and either way the point is that the reward is known to the one who receives it rather than strange. The next clause is what makes that reading necessary, "for they will be served fruit that looks similar but tastes different", so the likeness is in the eye and not on the tongue. Then "They will have pure spouses" and, at the end, "and they will be there forever", which is the longest clause in the passage and the reason it is called good news rather than a description. The sources ask how far the likeness may be read and answer that no one should take the picture apart, since what is given here is hope with a shape, and the verses after this return to the human being who has to decide.

**Good news, and for whom.**

(And give glad tidings unto those who believe) in Muhammad ﷺ and in the Qur'an (and do good works) of obedience that bind to their Lord; and it is also that this refers to doing any righteous deeds; (that theirs are Gardens beneath which), trees and habitations, (rivers flow) rivers of wine, milk, honey and water; (as often as they are provided with food), whenever they are fed in Paradise (of the fruit thereof) with different kinds of fruit, (they say: This is what was given us before), this is what we ate before, (and it is given to them) i.e. the food (in resemblance) as far as the colour is concerned but not the taste which is different. Give good news to those who have faith in Allah and do good, and tell them about that which will please them: gardens in Paradise, with rivers flowing beneath their palaces and trees. This verse is a caress for the friends, giving them hope for everlasting largesse and bliss, and an en couragement to the faithful, inciting them to obey and to seek increase of blessings. Let there be good news for all those who are today in the playing field of service, for tomorrow they will be in the assembly of repose and ease [56:89].

**Gardens under which rivers flow.**

Then He mentioned the favours enjoyed by the believers in Paradise, saying: They are the ones who shall be admitted into the gardens of Paradise. "This is what we were provided with before," and they will be given things in resemblance (i.e. in the same form but different in taste) and they shall have therein Azwajun Mutahharatun (purified mates or wives), and they will abide therein forever.

**Fruit that is known to the one who receives it.**

As for the fruits with which believers will be regaled in Paradise, some commentators say that this concerns only the fruits of Paradise which would be alike in shape, but each time different in taste. Thus, the fruits of Paradise13 may share a common name with the fruits of the earth, but they will be of a different nature. (and they will be given things in resemblance) means, "They look like each other, but the taste is different. " In another narration, Ibn 'Abbas said, "Only the names are similar between what is in this life and what is in Paradise." They will be given fruits that carry the same name and shape, so that they may recognise and desire them, but they will in fact taste differently. They will then be brought similar fruits, and the people of Paradise will comment, 'This is the same as what you have just brought us.' The boys will say to them, 'Eat, for the color is the same, but the taste is different.

**Pure spouses, and remaining forever.**

(There for them) in Paradise (are pure spouses), pure from menses or any kind of filth, (therein), in Paradise, (forever they abide) dwelling forever: never to die or be banished from it. In the Garden they will be paired with their mates, who will not have any unpleasant traits that people have on earth; and they will live there in eternal bliss, unlike the bliss of the earth which is only temporary.

**How far the likeness may be read.**

But no genuine Sufi has ever claimed that symbolical interpretation (I tibar) is the same thing as exegesis (tafsir), or that his own interpretation was exclusively the only valid one. In allowing for symbolical interpretations, we must carefully remember that since the Holy Qur'an has spoken of the fruits of Paradise and of similar things, they must have an objective existence, though not a physical one (in the current sense of the word), and even though we have no knowledge as to their nature and state - all of which we can safely leave to Allah Himself. The call of truth is indisputably marked with a divine radiance. The news is a caress for those it is given to, and the chapter now turns to the covenant.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Verse 24 spoke of the fire of hell which has been prepared to punish those who do not believe in the Holy Qur'an; the present verse announces the reward for those who believe. And when the Jews said ‘Why does God strike a similitude about flies where He says And if a fly should rob them of anything Q. 2273 and about a spider where He says As the likeness of the spider Q. 2941 what does God want with these vile creatures? Others say that these fruits would resemble the fruits of the earth in shape alone, but their taste would be totally different. Anyhow, the point is that the believers would have a kind of joy in Paradise they had never known before, and that this joy would keep renewing itself at every moment. Our modernists have for some time been quite fond of asserting that in speaking of the fruits of Paradise and its other joys, the Holy Qur'an has employed only a metaphysical mode of expression in order to suggest spiritual bliss which, by its very nature, is intangible. We do not mean to rule out the possibility or the desirability of analogical or symbolical interpretations of the verses of the Holy Qur'an. In fact, many authentic Muslim scholars, particularly the Sufis, have made such attempts which have proved to be very illuminating in many ways. The purpose of analogical interpretation has always been to serve as an aid in spiritual realization or in the elaboration of metaphysical doctrines, and not to negate or oppose the regular mode of exegesis. What our modern exegetes overlook in their zeal and in their simplicity is the obvious fact that if a thing is being used as a metaphor or a symbol, it does not necessarily argue that it does not exist objectively. That way lies security, for that is the Straight Path. The wives which the believers will have in Paradise, will be clean externally and pure internally - that is to say, free from everything that is physically disgusting like excrement and menstruation, and from everything that is morally disgusting like bad temper or unfaith fulness. The joys of Paradise will also be unlike the joys of the earth in that they will not be short-lived, nor will one have to be trembling with the fear of losing them, for the believers shall live in perpetual bliss forever.

26.text:
The chapter has just asked people to fear a fire, and now it answers a complaint about the style of the book itself: "Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller". The objection was that a divine book should not name so small a creature, and the verse replies by denying the shame rather than by explaining the gnat. The hearers are then divided, "As for the believers", "they know that it is the truth from their Lord", and "And as for the disbelievers, they argue", where the whole difficulty is one question, "What does Allah mean by such a parable" — an asking after an intention behind the words rather than after their truth, which is how a small creature becomes the test it is. The answer given is not about the insect but about what a test does, "Through this test", "He leaves many to stray", "and guides many", and then the limit of it, "And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious". The order of those three clauses is what the commentary works with, since one and the same thing, a parable in the ear of a hearer, becomes guidance to one person and error to another, and nothing in the wording has changed between the two hearings, and the word for the rebellious is a going beyond what was set for a person, so the straying is not caused by the parable but by what the hearer already was when it was recited to them. What is being settled here is the ground of the next two verses, which describe the people who go beyond, and then the question that is put to them.

**Why a gnat is named in a book.**

In the foregoing verses, it was affirmed that the Holy Qur'an does not admit of any kind of doubt, and that if someone should have a suspicion as to its being the Word of God, he should try to produce even a small Surah comparable to it. They had been saying that had the Qur'an been the Word of Allah, it would not have employed contemptible creatures like an ant or a gnat in its parables, for such a thing goes against the sublimity and majesty of Allah, when it would embarrass even a man with some sense of dignity. When Allah mentioned the flies and the spider in His Book, the people of misguidance said, 'Why did Allah mention these things.' So Allah revealed;. (Lo! Allah disdaineth not), He cannot abstain from coining similes, and how can He disdain mentioning something that if all created being were to join forces to create, they would not be able to do so. Allah does not disdain (to coin the similitude) Allah does not disdain explaining to people a similitude (even of a gnat), even regarding a gnat, (or what is above it) let alone a simile of something greater than a gnat such as a fly, or a spider.

**What the believers know about it.**

(Those who believe) in Muhammad and the Qur'an (know that it), the simile, (is the Truth from their Lord; but those who disbelieve), in Muhammad and the Qur'an, (say: What doth Allah wish (to teach) by such similitude?) say: The believers know and trust that there is wisdom in the use of such examples, while the disbelievers will make fun, asking each other why Allah uses examples with lowly creatures, such as gnats, flies and spiders. God then responds to them saying Thereby that is by this similitude He leads many astray from the truth on account of their disbelieving in it and thereby He guides many believers on account of their belief in it; and thereby He leads none astray except the wicked those that reject obedience to Him.

**What does such a parable mean.**

Allah replies that in these examples lie guidance, direction and a test for people. Since the matter can be described in this way He is not ashamed to strike a similitude of the gnat just as He is not ashamed to strike a similitude of the throne and what is below it. It is said that one aspect of the similitude of the gnat is the fact that when it is hungry it becomes strong and flies but once it is satiated it splits open and dies.

**Many led astray, and many guided.**

What Allah wishes by such simile is that (He misleadeth many thereby) of the Jews from the true Religion, (and He guideth many thereby) of the believers, (and He misleadeth thereby), by such similes, (only miscreants), the Jews. There are many people who are misguided by Allah through these examples, because they refuse to consider them; and there are many who He guides along the right path because they learn from them. It is said that or anything above it means a [larger] flying insect dhubāb. [Here] one aspect of the allusion is the insolence of the fly in that it keeps returning no matter how much it is driven away.

**The rebellious, and what the word covers.**

In the terminology of the Shari'ah, fisq signifies 'going beyond the circle of obedience to Allah, or transgressing the commandments of Allah'. That is to say, a man who commits a major sin and does not repent, or who insists on committing minor sins and makes it a habit, would be called a fasiq in the terminology of the Fuqaha'; on the other hand, a man who commits such sins publicly and openly without being ashamed of it is called a kafir . However, the Fisq of the disbeliever is worse, and this is the type of Fasiq that the Ayah is describing here, because Allah described them as,. The parable divides two kinds of hearer, and the next verse describes the second of them at length.

**What else the same passage holds.**

These two verses refer to an objection raised by the disbelievers with regard to the Holy Qur'an, and provide an answer to them. The Holy Qur'an points out that when one intends to speak of a detestable thing or person or situation, in a parable, the use of a gnat or something even more contemptible neither transgresses the principles of eloquence or logic, nor does it go against the sense of dignity or modesty, and hence Allah does not feel shy in using such imagery. The Holy Qur'an also shows that doubts of this kind arise only in the minds of those whom their disbelief has drained of all power to see things in a proper perspective, while such empty misgivings never touch the minds and hearts of true believers. The Holy Qur'an proceeds to suggest even a raison d'etre for the use of such parables: they serve as a test for men. In the case of those who are ready to think and to understand, they become a source of guidance; but for those who refuse to understand, out of indifference or out of a stubborn hostility and denial, they are a cause of greater confusion and misguidance. In elaborating this point, the Holy Qur'an specifies that these parables throw into confusion only those disobedient and rebellious people who disavow the covenant they have made with Allah, break all those relationships which Allah has commanded them to keep intact, and consequently produce an ever-widening disorder and anarchy in the world. The Arabic word used by the Holy Qur'an in speaking of the disobedient is Al-fasiqin, its root being fasaqa which means to go outside or to stray beyond a limit'. Now, transgression does not stop at being merely disobedient in one's actions, but can sometimes lead to outright denial and disbelief. So, the word fasiq is applied to a disbeliever (kafir) as well - such a use of the word is frequent in the Holy Qur'an. A Muslim who is a habitual sinner is also called a fasiq - this is how the jurists (Fuqaha') ordinarily use the word, making the fasiq a counterpart of the kafir on the opposite side. The Covenant which the transgressors disavow refers to the one that all men made with Allah before any of them came down to the earth. The Holy Qur'an says that Allah brought together the spirits of all men, and asked them: :"Am I not your Lord?

The chapter puts what follows as an astonishment rather than a refutation, "How can you deny Allah", and then gives four facts in answer to it: "You were lifeless and He gave you life", "then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life", and at the end "and then to Him you will all be returned". The sources stop on the order of the four, since a person is first nothing, then living, then dead, then living again, and only the last of these is asked of them, a returning which they had no part in bringing about. Then the word for lifeless is read as a thing with no claim to be counted at all, and the first giving of life is taken as the chief blessing, because nothing further can be demanded of a person who has not yet been given themselves. One commentary counts the deaths and the lives here and finds two of each, the first death being the state before birth, which is why the verse begins where nobody can dispute it, since a person cannot claim to have made themselves and cannot deny that they were made. The four are the same evidence the parable of the gnat was offered to, a book that names a small thing and the last day in the same confidence; and the verse after this widens from a person's own life to everything on the earth around them.

**You were lifeless.**

How do you people of Makkah disbelieve in God when you were dead semen inside loins and He gave you life in the womb and in this world by breathing Spirit into you the interrogative here is either intended to provoke amazement at their persistent unbelief despite the evidence established or intended as a rebuke; then He shall make you dead after your terms of life are completed then He shall give you life at the Resurrection then to Him you shall be returned! after resurrection whereupon He shall requite you according to your deeds; and He states as proof of the Resurrection when they denied it. According to this verse, the chief blessing of Allah for man is life, for without life he cannot profit from any other blessing. The first of these two verses refers to the blessings which are particular to the very being of man -- that is to say, he had no life before Allah gave him existence.

**Two deaths and two lives.**

Then He will give you death, then again will bring you to life (on the Day of Resurrection) and then unto Him you will return. (Then He will give you death) when your lifespan ends, (then life again) for the Resurrection, (and then unto Him ye will be returned) in the Hereafter whereupon He shall requite you for your works. Thus, the first 'death' or 'state of lifelessness' was at the beginning before man received life from Allah; the second death comes when a man completes the life-span allotted to him; and the second life will be given on the Day of Judgment. Then He shall make you dead, then He shall bring you to life.

**The life of fear and the life of hope.**

Life also is of three sorts: first the life of fear, then the life of hope, then the life of love. The life of fear appears in kindness, the life of hope appears in service, and the life of love appears in remembrance. But God has not just created man and left it at that:

**Returned, and asked for an account.**

Then you will return to Him and be held accountable. (How disbelieve you in Allah) how astonishing that you disbelieve in Allah (when you were dead) sperm drops in the loins of your fathers (and He gave life to you!) in the wombs of your mothers. **What else the same passage holds.**

The earlier verses affirmed the existence and the Oneness of Allah, and prophethood, giving self-evident proofs and refuting the whimsical and false notions of the doubters and the disbelievers. These two verses speak of the blessings which Allah has showered on man, pointing out that all the same there are men who do not recognize the bounty of Allah and persist in their denial -- the suggestion being that if they do not want to take the trouble of considering the arguments which have been advanced by the Holy Qur'an in the earlier verses, they should, as every man with an undistorted nature must, at least be grateful to their benefactor, for even this would be a way of realizing why they should be obedient to Allah. The second verse refers to the general blessings which are common to man and other creatures -- firstly, the earth and all that it contains and on which man's life immediately depends, and secondly, the skies with which life on earth is directly related. Verse 28 begins by expressing surprise at those who insist on being ungrateful to Allah and on denying Him. On the face of it, the disbelievers had never denied Allah but only the Holy Prophet all the same, the Holy Qur'an equates such a denial with the denial of Allah Himself. Then, the verse reminds man that once he was "dead" (amwat), or that he had no life. He existed, if at all, in the shape of billions of lifeless particles aimlessly floating; Allah brought them together, made them into a man, and gave them life. The verse proceeds to warn him that Allah will take away his life, and then give it back to him a second time. **What a person is given to use.**

There are things which man uses physically as food or medicine; other things are useful for him without his knowing it; even poisonous or dangerous things do him some good; even things which are forbidden for him in one of their aspects, may in some other aspect be quite beneficial; finally, almost everything can serve to teach him a lesson or illuminate him in the interest of his life in the Hereafter. On the basis of verse 29, some scholars have came to the conclusion that since everything in the world has been created for man, it is essentially legitimate (Halal) and permissible (Mubah) for man to make use of everything, except the things which have been forbidden by the Shari'ah.

**What turned towards the heaven means.**

He turned to the creation of the heaven, (and fashioned it as seven heavens) positioning them vertically above the earth.

**Seven heavens, one above the other.**

(And made them seven heavens) means, one above the other, while the 'seven earths' means, one below the other." Then, the verse speaks of the creation of the sky and its division into seven skies or heavens, as they are usually called in English. Verse 29 shows that the earth was created before the skies, as indicated by the word, :

**A favour great enough to ask for surrender.**

This is a favour great enough to make man completely surrender himself to God. He has given him an earth made to suit his needs perfectly. When you step into the street of My covenant, you do not know what good news reaches the heaven-dwellers and the earth-dwellers and how they congratulate each other. He is knower of all things, which is the clause the account of creation ends on here and the one the next verse assumes.

**What else the same passage holds.**

In recounting the blessings which man has received from Allah, verse 29 refers to Allah having created for man "all that the earth contains. " This small phrase comprehends all kinds of benefits which accrue to him from the earth and its produce. In this context, the Holy Qur'an uses the Arabic word, Istawa which initially means 'to stand upright, to climb', and thence signifies 'to turn or pay attention to something', and, in a wider sense, 'to take a straight and firm decision which nothing can hinder'. The implication here is that Allah being Omniscient and Omnipotent, it was not at all difficult for Him to create the universe, once He had decided to do so. Verse 28 shows that a man who does not apparently deny Allah, but refuses to accept the Holy Prophet as the Messenger of Allah, and the Holy Qur'an as the Book of Allah, would still be counted among those who do not believe in Allah. Verse 28 mentions only one kind of life which is to follow one's physical death - that is, the life which will begin on the Day of Resurrection - but says nothing about the life in the grave, although the Holy Qur'an and Hadith explicitly speak of how people will be questioned about their faith in their graves, and will also receive some reward or punishment. Now, this life in the grave is something intermediary (Barzakh) between the life which man has in this world and one he will have in the other. In other words, it is a state in between the two, resembling the life one has while dreaming; it can be called a supplement to the life of this world as also a prelude to the life hereafter. In short, this intermediary life is not in itself a distinct entity, and hence need not be mentioned separately. According to verse 29, everything in the universe has been created for man. It means that there is nothing in the universe from which man does not derive some benefit in one way or the other, directly or indirectly. The great Sufi Ibn Ata' remarks in connection with this verse: 'Allah has created the universe for you so that it should serve you and you should serve Allah. A wise man should thus know that he will certainly get what has been created for him, and should not, in worrying about it, forget the Being for whom he himself has been created' (Al-Bahr al-Muhit). So, the use of a thing is to be regarded as lawful so long as the Holy Qur'an or the Hadith does not forbid it.

30.text:
The chapter turns from what was made to what was said before the making, and it opens as a reminder rather than a story, "Remember when your Lord said to the angels", and then the announcement, "I am going to place a successive human authority on earth". The sources insist at once that no consultation is taking place, since the announcement is not a question, and so the reply of the angels is not a refusal but a thing they could not see past, "They asked Allah", "Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness, Allah responded". The verse attaches the reply to the question before a reader can let the question stand alone, and the sources take that placement as part of its sense, since the angels were not corrected for asking. The word for the authority is taken up next, because a person set over a thing is answerable for it, and the commentary takes the angels to have spoken out of what they knew of corruption, and they were not wrong about what it does. Then the answer, "Allah responded", "I know what you do not know", is the sentence the whole passage turns on, since it neither rebukes the question nor answers it, and one reading keeps the two halves of the exchange together, what was hidden from them being not the wickedness of mankind but what would come out of it. The sources also stop on the word "Remember", since the chapter is not informing the Prophet of something he did not know but turning him back to something already told, and the same word opens every one of these announcements in this sūrah. What is settled by the exchange is the standing of the person being announced, an authority that is answerable rather than a rank that is automatic, and that is why the angels are given a reply instead of an explanation. This is where the chapter begins its account of man, and the verses after it bring the names, the refusal to prostrate, and the command about the pair in the garden.

**What the word for authority carries.**

According to this usage, the word came to refer to one invested with power. When God created man to dwell on earth, He decreed that he might enjoy freedom of will. (Lo! I am about to place a vicegerent in the earth), I am creating a vicegerent from the earth, (they said: Wilt Thou place therein), will you create therein (one who will do harm therein) by committing sin (and will shed blood) through transgression, (while we, we hymn Thy praise), pray following Your command (and sanctify Thee) and mention you in a state of purity?

**No consultation took place.**

In fact, Allah did not mean to seek the advice of the angels, nor was there any need for it, but He, in His wisdom, gave a mere statement the form of a consultation in order to teach men the advisability of mutual consultation. He is the Lord and Master, and all His creatures, be they men or angels, are His slaves - no one has the right to question Him about His actions, and to ask Him why He did this or why He did not do that: : Allah tells His Prophet and humankind that He said to the angels that He would put humans on earth who will give birth to other humans, to inhabit it according to His laws.

**Why the angels asked.**

The angels submitted that they could not understand why men were being chosen to be-the deputies, for some of them would shed blood and spread disorder on this earth. They thought that they themselves were more suited to perform this function, as the nature of angels is wholly good, no evil deed can possibly come out of them, they are totally obedient to Allah, and should hence be more capable of managing the affairs of the world. The angels knew of this fact, according to their understanding of human nature, for Allah stated that He would create man from clay. What is the wisdom of creating such creatures since they will cause trouble in the earth and spill blood?

**I know what you do not know, and what they did not.**

(He said: Surely I know that) which shall ensue from this vicegerent (which you know not). Allah replied to their question, saying that He knew the deep wisdom behind His creation of them, and behind making them guardians, and the angels did not. And when thy Lord said to the angels, "Surely I am setting in the earth a vicegerent," they said, "What, wilt Thou set therein one who will work corruption there, and shed blood, while we glorify Thy praise and call Thee holy? They said ‘God will never create anything more noble in His eyes than us nor more knowledgeable since we have been created before it and have seen what it has not seen. Speaking according to their own lights, they very humbly submitted that a creature like man who carried within himself a tendency towards evil and disorder and who would not balk even at blood-shed, could not be expected to maintain peace and order on the earth, while they themselves, being free of all evil, and perfect in their obedience and devotion, could perform the function more satisfactorily. The angels asked their Lord, trying to understand, what the wisdom behind making the children of Adam guardians of the earth was, when they would ruin things in it, and kill in it, while the angels always do as He tells them, and recognise His greatness, praising Him and honouring His power and perfection.

**What the announcement did to them.**

When the angels heard this terrifying declaration, settledness and repose fled from them and they lost the composure of their intellects and their patience. But He had a particular reason for investing man with power and freedom on earth. If many human beings were to be corrupted by their power, there would also be a substantial number who, in spite of their power and freedom on earth, would acknowledge God’s greatness and power and their own helplessness. Adam was formed from the surface of the earth, and the chapter goes on from here to teach him names rather than to defend its choice.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The preceding verses recounted the general and some of the particular blessings of Allah, and asked man to recognize them and not to be ungrateful and disobedient to his Benefactor. Now, ten verses, beginning with the 30th, tell the story of the father of mankind, Adam in continuation of this theme and also by way of illustration. God then created Adam from the surface of the earth adīm al-ard adīm literally means ‘skin’ taking a handful of all its colours and mixing it with different waters then made him upright and breathed into him the Spirit and he thus became a living being with senses after having been inanimate. For, blessings are of two kinds - tangible and intangible. Food, water, money, houses, or lands are some of the tangible blessings; while honour, happiness or knowledge are intangible ones. The earlier verses were concerned with blessings of the first kind; these verses speak of those of the second kind - that is to say, how Allah bestowed the gift of knowledge on Adam made the angels prostrate themselves before him to show their respect, and gave men the honour of being his sons. The present three verses relate how Allah, having decided to create Adam and to make him His deputy on the earth, spoke of it to the angels - seemingly by way of a trial, suggesting that they should express their opinions in this matter. In replying to them, Allah first adopted the mode of authority, and told the angels that they knew nothing about the nature and the needs of deputation on the earth, and that Allah alone was the one to know it fully. The second answer was in the mode of wisdom – Adam had been given preference over the angels on account of his superiority in the station of knowledge, because in order to function properly as a deputy on the earth one must know the names, the properties and the characteristics of the things to be found there, and the angels had no aptitude for this kind of knowledge.

31.text:
The verse takes the test out of the angels' hands and puts it in Adam's, and it does so in four moves that have to be kept in order. First, "He taught Adam the names of all things", with the teaching before any claim of rank, so the advantage is described as something given and not something earned, and the names are his by the same route the gnat in the earlier parable is a sign, by being told. Then "then He presented them to the angels and said", which is the turn: the parade is for the angels, not for information. "Tell Me the names of these" is a command addressed to them, and the sources notice that the wording is an invitation to admit what they had said. "if what you say is true" closes the test with the condition, and it is the clause the commentators work with here, since the demand is only for a recital of the names and they have already been told the reason they were asked.

**What was taught first.**

And He taught Adam the names that is the names of things named all of them by placing knowledge of them into his heart; then He presented them these names the majority of which concerned intellectual beings to the angels and said to them in reproach ‘Now tell Me inform Me the names of these things named if you speak truly’ in your claim that I would not create anything more knowledgeable than you or that you are more deserving of this vicegerency; the response to the conditional sentence is intimated by what precedes it. To reveal the position of Adam, Allah taught him the names of everything, living things and objects, their pronunciation and meanings.

**Why the angels were asked.**

**The parade and its point.**

Allah's statement means, "Tell Me the names of what I paraded before you, O angels who said,. Then he put them before the angels, instructing them to tell Him the names if they were telling the truth when they said that they were a nobler and better creation than Adam. Can you give me the name of each one of them, and say what sort of people they will be?

**What the mode of expression shows.**

" The difference in the mode of expression shows that Adam was given the rank of a teacher, and the angels that of pupils. Just as He taught [Adam] the names of created things-all of them according to what is articulated in the tafsīr of Ibn ʿAbbās and others-He also taught him the names of the Real .

Another thing the episode indicates is that an increase or decrease is possible in the degree of knowledge the angels possess, for they were given, through Adam at least a primary knowledge about a thing which they did not know before. But He only disclosed to [the angels] the locus He chose for knowledge of the names of created things and by that [disclosure] the measure of [Adam's] superiority over them. It is said [that in the words] then He presented them the [word] then thumma is a particle of extension or delay. Then God told Adam their names and characteristics, and then commanded him to pass the knowledge on to the angels.

**What else the same passage holds.**

And He taught Adam all the names (of everything), then He showed them to the angels and said, "Tell Me the names of these if you are truthful. "Glory is to You, we have no knowledge except what you have taught us. Inform them of their names," and when he had informed them of their names, He said: "Did I not tell you that I know the Ghayb (unseen) in the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you have been concealing? This episode, according to Imam al-Ash'ari shows that language as such has been created by Allah Himself, and not invented by man - its use by different kinds of men has later on produced the many forms of language. One should note a subtle suggestion here in the use of two words. 32.text:
The reply is the whole lesson, and the order it comes in is why it is quoted in every discussion of etiquette afterwards. "They replied, Glory be to You" puts the exalting before anything is told about themselves, and the sources read that as the proper shape of an answer when a person has been shown to be short of knowledge: speak first about God, not about the case. "We have no knowledge except what You have taught us" then concedes the point the test was built to make, and the wording is careful, since they do not claim that knowledge is bad but that none of it is theirs except what has been given. "You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise" ends with a description of God rather than an apology for themselves, and the emphatic construction in that clause is what one commentary stops on. The verse before had exposed a claim to know, and this is the opposite posture, drawn from the angels themselves, set down for any hearer who is asked something beyond them.

**Glory be to You.**

They said ‘Glory be to You! exalting You above that any should object to You We know not except what You have taught us. (They said: Be glorified!), we repent to you of what we said (We have no knowledge saving that which Thou hast taught us), inspired us with.

Surely You are innaka anta emphasises the preceding suffixed pronoun kāf the Knower Wise’ from whose knowledge and wisdom nothing escapes. (Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Knower) of us and of them (the Wise) regarding our matters and theirs. **The claim a person has no leave to make.**

For example, no man should take the life of another: all actions of this nature disqualify mankind from receiving God’s mercy. **What the Knower Wise means in the reply.**

Surely You are the Knower Wise. [The angels] offered praise before they made their apology and declared the truth of His judgment over any objection they might have. Surely You are the Knower Wise that is what You do is true and sincere there is none who can pass judgment over You and there is no foolishness nor ugliness from You. 33.text:
The verse has three clauses and each one changes who is speaking, so the guidance is in following that. "Allah said, O Adam" is the address, and the sources point out that Adam is named while the angels are still the ones being tested, so the teaching is shown to be a trust rather than a superiority. "Inform them of their names" tells him to speak to the angels, which is the reversal of the previous verse, since they had been told to recite and could not. "Then when Adam did, Allah said" passes over the recital itself in four words, and the commentaries are aware of how quickly it is done, the point being the obedience and not the list. "Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth" then returns to the angels, with the question addressed to them about what they had said earlier, and "and I know what you reveal and what you conceal" then covers the part of their case that no parade of names could touch, so the verse closes on what was in their hearts rather than on what they had said out loud. The commentaries use the sequence to make two points at once, that knowledge is given and not inherited, and that the one who receives it is answerable for it, which is the same order the parable of the gnat had set, a small thing taught and a claim examined. The names themselves are left unspecified in the verse, and the sources list what they were taken to cover, so nothing here turns on settling which of the things in the parade was meant. The verse after this turns from knowledge to command, and the prostration that is refused.

He exalted be He said ‘Adam tell them the angels their names’ all of the things named; so he named each thing by its appellation and mentioned the wisdom behind its creation; And when he had told them their names He exalted said in rebuke ‘Did I not tell you that I know the Unseen in the heavens and the earth? what is unseen in them And I know what you reveal what you manifested when you said ‘What will You appoint therein …’ and what you were hiding what you were keeping secret when you were saying that God would not create anything more knowledgeable or more noble in His eyes than us.
